title: The Made-Up Word That Got Me Into Trouble
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman explains why he is sceptical of England's current push for oracy. He begins with Andrew Wilkinson's coining of the word in 1965 to put speaking and listening on a par with literacy and numeracy, and argues the three are not alike because speech is biologically primary while reading and writing must be taught with effort in schools. He is also wary of invented abstract nouns generally, tolerating literacy but doubting numeracy, which he sees as a label that mainly supports the contextualisation of mathematics favoured by progressivists. His worry is that oracy will serve as cover for faddish teaching and a return to the progressive inspection regime, and he notes its link to Voice 21, spun out of the failed School 21. After an exchange on social media in which critics said all words are made up, he distinguishes naturally evolved words like speak from words coined to raise a concept's profile. He concludes that oracy certainly is a made-up word.
points: Ashman argues that oracy differs from literacy and numeracy because speaking and listening are biologically primary, whereas reading and writing need effortful instruction in schools.
He is wary of newly coined education terms, suspecting they are used to reheat simple ideas and sell them to a credulous public.
Numeracy, in his reading, is a label whose only distinctive feature is requiring maths to be set in forced, mundane contexts, advancing progressive contextualisation.
His main concern is that the oracy push will be cover for faddish teaching, with Voice 21's origins in School 21 feeding that suspicion.
He draws a line between words that evolved over time, such as speak, and words invented in the 1960s to boost a concept's prestige.
quotes: The problem is that literacy, numeracy and oracy are not the same. As Wilkinson himself points out, oracy is ‘a skill which everybody is exercising most of the time’.

We have therefore not evolved to pick up these skills with ease from the environment. Learning them requires significant effort and that seems to be why we created specialist institutions—schools—to teach these skills.
So however important you believe speaking and listening to be—and I do believe they are important and should be developed in schools—they are qualitatively different skills from reading and writing.
The only factor I can see is a disdain for abstract problems, instead requiring questions to be set in forced, mundane contexts.
This is one reason why I am sceptical of the current ‘oracy’ push in England. It is probably going to be used as cover for a whole load of faddish teaching.

Often this new label is a more complex one or sounds more scientific and my suspicion is that it is a device for reheating and selling relatively simple ideas, either to an academic readership or a credulous public.
I don’t think it is meaningful to say a word like ‘speak’ is made up. If I claimed this in an everyday context, people would think I was being daft.
